Respiratory metabolism in the common opossum (Didelphis marsupialis) has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions to establish its maximum basal metabolic rate. At an ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], adult individuals exhibit a resting oxygen consumption of 611.30 milliliters per hour [JOi = 611.30 milliliters per hour], a value that reflects the relatively low metabolic intensity characteristic of marsupials compared to similar-sized eutherian mammals. This measurement was obtained from post-absorptive, inactive animals during their inactive photophase, ensuring that the recorded rate approximates true basal conditions. The thermoneutral zone for this species appears to center near this temperature, as deviations from 35 °C elicit measurable increases in metabolic rate associated with thermoregulatory costs. These data provide a physiological baseline for understanding how Didelphis marsupialis allocates energetic resources across its life cycle, particularly during periods of reproductive investment and lactation.

Female common opossums produce litters of 6 pups [N_R_i = 6 pups] per reproductive event and typically complete 2 litters each year [F_R_i = 2 litters each year], a reproductive strategy that balances relatively high offspring number against the energetic demands of extended lactation in a seasonal environment. When maintained at an environmental temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], this annual fecundity schedule yields a substantial total reproductive output, with females investing heavily in each litter over a prolonged period of pouch life and subsequent nursing. The neonatal mass at birth is remarkably modest, with newborns weighing only 0.13 grams [Wwb = 0.13 grams], an extreme altricial condition that is typical of marsupials and reflects the abbreviated gestation period. This tiny birth mass necessitates a long and energetically costly period of maternal care within the pouch, where the altricial neonate undergoes most of its morphological development while attached to a teat.

Gestation in the common opossum is remarkably brief, lasting only 12 days [tg = 12 days] at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], representing one of the shortest gestation durations recorded among mammals relative to maternal body size. This abbreviated intrauterine development results in the delivery of profoundly altricial neonates, each weighing a mere fraction of a gram, as described above. Following parturition, the nursing offspring remain continuously attached to the mother's teats for a period of about 178 days since birth [tx = about 178 days since birth] at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], at which point weaning occurs and the juveniles transition to independent foraging. This extended weaning period is considerably longer than the 90 to 125 days reported in some other sources, suggesting that local environmental conditions or maternal nutritional status may influence the precise timing of nutritional independence. The prolonged lactation phase imposes substantial energetic costs on the breeding female.

Sexual maturity in Didelphis marsupialis is attained at approximately 200 days since birth [tp = approximately 200 days since birth] when individuals are maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a developmental milestone that corresponds to roughly 6 to 7 months of age under favorable nutritional conditions. This timing aligns with the attainment of near-adult body dimensions and the onset of reproductive cyclicity in both sexes. The ultimate wet weight for adult females reaches an average of 1030 grams [Wwi = 1030 grams], while males attain a larger average ultimate wet weight of 1200 grams [Wwi = 1200 grams], reflecting a moderate degree of sexual size dimorphism that is common among didelphid marsupials. This size difference may be related to male-male competition for access to receptive females during the breeding season, as larger males often have greater success in securing mating opportunities.

Maximum lifespan in the common opossum has been estimated at approximately 4.2 years [am = approximately 4.2 years] when measured under controlled conditions at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This relatively short life expectancy, characteristic of small-to-medium-sized marsupials, reflects a fast-paced life history strategy in which early and prolific reproduction compensates for elevated rates of adult mortality from predation, disease, and environmental stochasticity. The species exhibits rapid growth through the juvenile phase, with young attaining independence and dispersing within the first year. Reproductive senescence has not been extensively documented in wild populations, but captive data suggest that fecundity may decline gradually after the second or third year, consistent with the general mammalian pattern of age-related reproductive decline.
